  1668	  difference morphism \(J_s\times J_s\to J_s\), so the group scheme is separated.
  1669	
  1670	  Choose a point of \(C\) over the separably closed base and use its \(g(C)\)-fold divisor to
  1671	  translate the degree-\(g(C)\) Abel map to \(\mathrm{pic}^0(C)\).  After any algebraically
  1672	  closed extension, Riemann--Roch gives a section of every degree-\(g(C)\) line bundle, so this
  1673	  translated Abel map \(D_g\to J_s\) is surjective.  It is proper because \(D_g\) is projective
  1674	  and \(J_s\) is separated.  A surjective image of the quasi-compact scheme \(D_g\) makes
  1675	  \(J_s\) quasi-compact; combined with local finite type, this gives finite type.  Properness
  1676	  descends through the surjective proper map: after every base change, the image in the base
  1677	  of a closed subset of \(J_s\) is the image of its closed inverse image in \(D_g\), hence is
  1678	  closed.  Finally, the geometric fibres of \(D_g\) are irreducible by
  1679	  Theorem~\ref{thm:genusDivisorSource_geometry}, and their surjective images are irreducible.
  1680	  These are exactly the certificates required by the package.
  1681	\end{proof}
  1682	
  1683	\begin{theorem}[Limit and faithfully flat compatibility of \(\mathrm{pic}^0\)]
  1684	  \label{thm:pic0DescentCompatibility}
  1685	  \provenancetag{CUSTOM}
  1686	  \uses{def:pic0Functor}
  1687	  \notready
  1688	  The degree-zero etale Picard functor commutes with filtered unions of field extensions and
  1689	  satisfies effective descent along faithfully flat field extensions, compatibly with its
  1690	  universal classes.
  1691	\end{theorem}
  1692	\begin{proof}
  1693	  An invertible sheaf is given on a finite affine cover by finitely many finitely presented
  1694	  rank-one modules, transition isomorphisms, and finitely many cocycle equations.  All this
  1695	  data, as well as an isomorphism between two such data, descends to a finite stage of a
  1696	  filtered union.  The degree-zero condition is preserved and reflected after field extension
  1697	  because degree is invariant under scalar extension.  This proves filtered compatibility.
  1698	  Faithfully flat descent for finitely presented modules descends the local line bundles and
  1699	  their transition maps, while the cocycle equation gives effectivity and uniqueness.  Passing
  1700	  to the quotient by line bundles from the base and then to the etale sheafification preserves
  1701	  this descent statement, since both equivalence and effectivity may be checked after a common
  1702	  faithfully flat refinement.
  1703	\end{proof}
  1704	
  1705	\begin{theorem}[A finite Galois stage for the Picard representer]
  1706	  \label{thm:pic0FiniteGaloisStage}
  1707	  \provenancetag{CUSTOM}
  1708	  \uses{def:pic0SepClosedDescentInput, thm:pic0SepClosedDescentInput_exists,
  1709	    thm:pic0DescentCompatibility}
  1710	  \notready
  1711	  Let \(k^s\) be a separable closure of \(k\).  The separably closed descent package descends
  1712	  to a finite Galois extension \(L/k\): there are a finite-type proper group scheme \(J_L\)
  1713	  representing \(\mathrm{pic}^0(C_L)\), its universal class, and a semilinear action of
  1714	  \(\operatorname{Gal}(L/k)\) preserving that class and satisfying the cocycle condition.
  1715	  Every orbit of this action is contained in an affine open of \(J_L\).
  1716	\end{theorem}
  1717	\begin{proof}
  1718	  Because \(J_{k^s}\) is of finite presentation, it descends to a finite subextension
  1719	  \(L_0/k\).  The universal class descends after enlarging \(L_0\), by
  1720	  Theorem~\ref{thm:pic0DescentCompatibility}.  The natural transformation defined by the
  1721	  descended class becomes the given representation after extension to \(k^s\); faithful flat
  1722	  descent for both the Yoneda functor and the Picard sheaf shows that it is already an
  1723	  isomorphism over \(L_0\).  Properness, the group operations, and their finitely many axioms
  1724	  also descend after one further finite extension.  Enlarge \(L_0\) to a finite Galois
  1725	  extension \(L/k\).
  1726	
  1727	  For \(\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(L/k)\), both \(\sigma^*J_L\) and \(J_L\), equipped with
  1728	  their transported universal classes, represent the same functor.  Yoneda uniqueness gives
  1729	  a unique semilinear isomorphism between them.  The two composites associated to
  1730	  \(\sigma\tau\) carry the universal class to the same element, so uniqueness proves the
  1731	  cocycle equation.  A proper finite-type group scheme over a field is projective.  Given a
  1732	  finite Galois orbit, choose a closed specialization of each of its finitely many points.
  1733	  For a sufficiently high power of an ample line bundle, restriction of global sections to
  1734	  the resulting finite closed subscheme is surjective.  Lift the section that is \(1\) at
  1735	  every member of that subscheme.  Its nonvanishing locus contains the chosen closed
  1736	  specializations and therefore the original orbit; as the complement of an ample effective
  1737	  divisor, this locus is affine.  This proves the final certificate.
  1738	\end{proof}
  1739	
  1740	\begin{lemma}[Stable affine neighbourhoods for a finite action]
  1741	  \label{lem:finiteGalois_stableAffineCover}
  1742	  \provenancetag{CUSTOM}
  1743	  \notready
  1744	  Let a finite group \(G\) act on a separated scheme \(X\).  If every \(G\)-orbit is contained
  1745	  in an affine open, then \(X\) has a \(G\)-stable affine open cover.

name: horizon-waiting
description: How to wait for slow work (builds, subagents, monitors) inside a one-shot session — block in the foreground and get the result before you report; you are NEVER re-invoked on completion.
---

Your session is **one-shot and headless**. When you write your final report the
session ENDS and nothing calls you back. There is no notification when a
background job finishes, and any process you backgrounded is killed the moment
the session exits. So a plan like "kick off the build and wait to be notified"
silently fails: the notification never comes and the build dies with you.

Therefore, whenever a result you depend on is produced by a build, subagent,
monitor, or shell command:

- **Run it in the FOREGROUND and block on it.** Wait for it to finish and read
  its exit code / output within this session. A heavy `lake build` can take many
  minutes (sometimes 20+) — budget for that and wait it out; do not cut it short.
- If you must poll, **poll in a loop inside this session** until the work has
  definitively finished. Never end the session expecting to resume.
- Do **not** end with phrases like "monitoring stopped; it will notify me on
  completion", "still compiling, will report when done", or "I'll pick this up
  next session". There is no next invocation of *this* session.

If the work genuinely cannot finish in the time you have:

- Do NOT imply success or write a conclusion that assumes a pending result.
- Under `## Issues`, record exactly what is still running/unknown and why.
- Leave the explicit next action for a future run to pick up.

The one thing worse than a slow session is a session that reports a green result
it never actually observed. Get the result, or say clearly that you didn't.
